### Problem: First Missing Positive {#sec-lts-p2-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Given an unsorted integer array `nums` ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $-2^{31} \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 2^{31}-1$ — negatives and huge values allowed), return the smallest positive integer not present. The demand is explicit: $O(n)$ **time** and $O(1)$ **auxiliary space**.

Source: [LC 41 · First Missing Positive](https://leetcode.com/problems/first-missing-positive/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}

Example — `nums = [3, 4, -1, 1]`. Output `2` (1 is present, 2 is not).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The answer is always in $[1, n+1]$: among $n$ cells at most $n$ distinct positives $1..n$ fit, so if all of them appear the gap is $n+1$. That bounds the search to the array's own size — and therefore lets us *store the answer set inside the array*. Cyclic sort does it: value $v \in [1, n]$ belongs at index $v-1$, so swap each into place; the first index holding the wrong value names the missing number. Unlike @sec-lts-p2-a, values here can fall outside $[1, n]$, so we only place the ones in range.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Set scan.** Put everything in a hash set, then test $1, 2, 3, \dots$ until one is absent. $O(n)$ time but $O(n)$ space — breaks the space rule; the oracle.
2. **Cyclic placement.** Walk indices; while `nums[i]` is in $[1, n]$ and its home slot doesn't already hold it, swap it home. Afterwards the first $i$ with `nums[i] != i+1` gives the answer, else $n+1$. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space.

**Invariant.** Each successful swap puts one value permanently at its correct index (it is never touched again, since it is already home), so the loop performs at most $n$ swaps in total; when it ends, `nums[i] == i+1` exactly for the present values $1..n$.
:::

The buttons are in order: pay $O(n)$ memory for a set, then fold the set into the array with swaps.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Set scan

::: {.form-next}
Hash the values, then march an integer upward from $1$ and stop at the first not in the set. Correct in $O(n)$ time, but $O(n)$ space the problem forbids.

**Worked example.** seen $= \{-1, 1, 3, 4\}$; test $1$ (yes), $2$ (no) → answer $2$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("fmiss", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def fmp41_set(nums):
    seen = set(nums)
    ans = 1
    while ans in seen:
        ans += 1
    return ans
```

##### C++

```cpp
// hash the values, scan upward from 1; O(n) time but O(n) space
int fmp41Set(vector<int> nums) {
    unordered_set<int> seen(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    int ans = 1;
    while (seen.count(ans)) ++ans;
    return ans;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The `while ans in seen` can test at most $n+1$ values, so this is $O(n)$, not $O(n^2)$. Its only crime is the `unordered_set`, which the constraint rules out — the reason the placement form exists.

#### Cyclic placement (O(1) space)

::: {.form-next}
Send every in-range value to its home index $v-1$ by swapping; leave out-of-range values ($\le 0$ or $> n$) where they are. Then read the array as a truth table: index $i$ holds $i+1$ iff that number was present. The first mismatch is the gap. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space.

**Worked example.** $[3,4,-1,1] \to [1,-1,3,4]$ after placement; index 1 holds $-1 \ne 2$ → answer $2$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("fmiss", "cyclic")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-41-cyclic
def fmp41_cyclic(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    a = list(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        while 1 <= a[i] <= n and a[a[i] - 1] != a[i]:
            j = a[i] - 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    for i in range(n):
        if a[i] != i + 1:
            return i + 1
    return n + 1

for _ in range(400):
    x = [random.randint(-8, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 15))]
    assert fmp41_cyclic(x) == fmp41_set(x)
assert fmp41_cyclic([1, 2, 0]) == 3
assert fmp41_cyclic([3, 4, -1, 1]) == 2
assert fmp41_cyclic([7, 8, 9, 11, 12]) == 1
assert fmp41_cyclic([1, 2, 3]) == 4
print("fmp41_cyclic OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// cyclic sort into index v-1; O(n) time, O(1) space
int fmp41Cyclic(vector<int> nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        while (nums[i] >= 1 && nums[i] <= n && nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i])
            swap(nums[i], nums[nums[i] - 1]);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        if (nums[i] != i + 1) return i + 1;
    return n + 1;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The guard `a[a[i]-1] != a[i]` is what keeps the loop finite: if the home slot already holds this value (a duplicate), swapping would spin forever, so we stop. The `while` (not `if`) is needed because the value swapped *in* may itself need placement. Total swaps are bounded by $n$ since each settles one element for good. The `[-8, 12]` stress range deliberately throws in negatives, zeros, and values past $n$ to confirm they are simply ignored, and `[1,2,3]` proves the "everything $1..n$ present → $n+1$" fallthrough.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Set scan** is $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. **Cyclic placement** is $O(n)$ time (at most $n$ swaps across all `while` loops), $O(1)$ extra space — the only form that satisfies both demanded bounds.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All present as a permutation `[1..n]` → $n+1$.
- No positives at all (negatives/zero) → $1$ immediately.
- Duplicates (`[1,1]`) → the guard prevents an infinite swap; answer $2$.
:::

- [LC 287 · Find the Duplicate Number](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-duplicate-number/){difficulty="Medium"} — values in $[1, n]$ again, but the array may not be modified: the value-as-index idea becomes a linked list to walk.
:::
